q-83709.name: Question 1
q-83709.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-5$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}a & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & b \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & c\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}a & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & b \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
q-83709.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-5,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=-5.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=-2,$ $b=0,$ and $c=-5.$

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=5, λ2=−1, λ3=−5 are eigenvalues, and v1=[−2−22],v2=[121],v3=[20−1] are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of a,b,c given that A=[a12−22b21−1][5000−1000c][a12−22b21−1]−1?

a
a=−2, b=0, and c=−5
b
a=1, b=2, and c=5
c
a=−5, b=2, and c=0
d
a=−1, b=0, and c=5
e
a=2, b=1, and c=5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=5, λ2=−1, λ3=−5, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[5000−1000−5].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=5,

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−1, and

  • the 3rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ3=−5.

Therefore, we get

P=[−212−22021−1].

Finally, we obtain

A=[−212−22021−1][5000−1000−5][−212−22021−1]−1.

In conclusion, we get a=−2, b=0, and c=−5.

q-37806.name: Question 2
q-37806.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
q-37806.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=−3, λ2=1, λ3=−1 are eigenvalues, and v1=[20−1],v2=[−210],v3=[103] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[−30001000−1] and P=[1−2201030−1]
b
D=[2−21010−103] and P=[−30001000−1]
c
D=[21−2001−130] and P=[−30001000−1]
d
D=[−30001000−1] and P=[21−2001−130]
e
D=[−30001000−1] and P=[2−21010−103]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=−3, λ2=1, λ3=−1, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[−30001000−1].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=−3,

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=1, and

  • the 3rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ3=−1.

Therefore, we get

P=[2−21010−103].

q-37846.name: Question 3
q-37846.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -9 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
q-37846.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -9-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & 4 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-16) & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -15) & =0 \\ (-9-\lambda )(\lambda +3)(\lambda -5) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Note that all $\lambda $'s are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial.

Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

q-37843.name: Question 4
q-37843.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
q-37843.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -4 \\ -1 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(\lambda -1)(\lambda +3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-3.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

q-37843.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the matrix A, given by A=[−10−4−121−10−1]. Determine whether A=PDP−1 for some invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D, where P and D are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix D.

a
D=[20001000−3]
b
D=[100020003]
c
D=[−3000−1000−2]
d
D=[2000−10003]
e
D=[20001000−6]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to determine whether D is diagonalizable over R.

We start by computing the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

det(A−λI)=0|−1−λ0−4−12−λ1−10−1−λ|=0(2−λ)|−1−λ−4−1−1−λ|=0(2−λ)((−1−λ)(−1−λ)−4)=0(2−λ)(λ2+2λ−3)=0(2−λ)(λ−1)(λ+3)=0

Therefore, the eigenvalues of A are λ1=2, λ2=1, and λ3=−3. Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, A is diagonalizable.

We construct a diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix D is D=[20001000−3].

Note that the diagonal matrix D is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

[10002000−3].

q-40161.name: Question 5
q-40161.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & ∗ \\ 0 & 1 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the third column of the matrix $P.$
q-40161.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Computing $A-(4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{3}I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-(4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix $M$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix is already  in row echelon form.  It has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.  From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{2}(-4({x}_{3})-6{x}_{3}) \\  & =5{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

q-37848.name: Question 6
q-37848.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & a & -2 \\ -1 & b & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $(a+b)^{2}.$
q-37848.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{2}I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 12 & -10 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st  and the $2$nd ones). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get  ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $(a+b)^{2}=(0+1)^{2}=1.$

q-84611.name: Question 7
q-84611.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
q-84611.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

q-140262.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 \\ 5 & 4 & -5 \\ -5 & -5 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
q-140262.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -2 \\ 5 & 5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -2 \\ 5 & 3 & -5 \\ -5 & -5 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -5 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -2 & -2 \\ 5 & -5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

A=[1−2−254−5−5−54] The matrix A has eigenvalues λ1=−1, λ2=1, and λ3=9. Find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[−100010009] and P=[12001−1101]
b
D=[1000−1000−9] and P=[1800−5−1151]
c
A is not diagonalizable
d
D=[1000−1000−9] and P=[12001−1101]
e
D=[−100010009] and P=[1800−5−1151]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix:

λ1=−1, λ2=1, λ3=9.

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A. Applying our usual method, we get the following.

  • For λ1=−1, we get A−(−1)I=[2−2−255−5−5−55]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−1)I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v1=[101].

  • For λ2=1, we get A−1I=[0−2−253−5−5−53]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−1I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v2=[8−55].

  • For λ3=9, we get A−9I=[−8−2−25−5−5−5−5−5]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−9I)x=0 gives us the eigenvector v3=[0−11].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[−100010009],P=[1800−5−1151]
